title: Stack: hardware, identity and attention — what was ahead of its time
subtitle: 13 cards on top of the archive: FeliCa and QR, ucode, iAPX 432, Transputer, Setun, MSX and PC-98, TRON Code, NeWS, Weiser's calm technology — plus a build card “a device and protocol that survive”.
about: A stack about the physical layer and attention: capability rights in silicon, offline payment as infrastructure, an identifier without a vendor, ternary arithmetic, “send a program, not a picture”, and the rule of when an agent stays silent. Every card rests on a verified archive entry.

home.title: Hardware and attention: eleven decisions still worth using
home.subtitle: stack home · 13 cards · archive 1958–2026

fields.val: This stack is about what cannot be rewritten in software later: rights in silicon, offline transactions, an object identifier, response time, the shape of a character. Here are eleven decisions — from ternary Setun to Weiser's calm technology — and one control case of how an idea survives: the QR code, which was open and cheap.

Cards on the left, ← → pages through. Every card links to an archive entry (⌗) and to related cards; the reverse side of each link is visible under “links here”. The last card is the build card: eleven decisions to test your own device or protocol against.

Not a catalogue of retro hardware and not a forecast. Facts (years, numbers, names) come from verified archive entries; “what to build” and the “gap” score are the agent's judgement, marked as judgement.

qr.title: The QR code — the control case: how an idea survives
qr.subtitle: 1994 — present · Denso Wave · an open licence

fields.val: Denso Wave, 1994: a team of two engineers and eighteen months of work on a code holding about 7,000 digits, supporting kanji and reading more than ten times faster than existing symbologies.
The priorities matched a real task (capacity, speed, Japanese text) — and openness: the company did not restrict its use.
On the museum dashboard the QR code stands as a control case: of the Japanese ideas, the ones that survived were open and cheap; the ones that died were closed and vertically integrated.

The lesson for agent and IoT standards: an open licence and a low entry bar matter more than technical superiority. The acceptance criterion is a minimal core implemented over a weekend on cheap hardware.

links.pc98: the opposite outcome: a closed ecosystem

fields.val: Sony's contactless IC cards: Suica (JR East), Octopus (Hong Kong), EZ-Link; from 2004 Osaifu-Keitai — mobile FeliCa inside a phone.
National payment and access infrastructure: deterministic tap latency, offline operation, cryptography in the chip, EAL4 certification (later EAL6).

fields.lbl: Why it did not go global
fields.val: NFC-A/B (MIFARE) became the world standard by volume and price; FeliCa stayed largely an Asian technology, although it is part of NFC Forum requirements and Apple added it to Apple Pay in 2016 (iPhone 7 / Watch Series 2).
Alive in Japan and Asia as the native transit and payment infrastructure.

Treat payment and access as physical infrastructure rather than an application: offline transactions, hard latency guarantees, certified hardware. Applicable to offline payments, transit, and “tap-to-X” for IoT and agents.

links.build: the third build decision: offline and deterministic latency

other.pre-web/minitel: another example of a country's payment infrastructure: kiosque

actions.p: Design an offline transaction for an agent/device: limits, cryptography in the chip, behaviour when the link is lost, how to revoke. Start from FeliCa and Minitel's kiosque.

actions.p: Collect the facts: how FeliCa differs from NFC-A/B, where it is standardised, which devices carry it. Links to specifications and sources.

ucode.title: ucode — “DNS for things”, never built
ucode.subtitle: 2003 — present · T-Engine / uID Center · a 128-bit object ID

fields.val: A 128-bit identifier of physical objects (ucode), independent of the carrier technology (RFID, barcode, matrix code), plus a ucodeRP resolution server, a ubiquitous communicator and information servers. The uID Center was led by Ken Sakamura.
“DNS for things”: the identifier is separated both from the carrier and from the application; two-stage resolution (code → resolution server → data) is exactly what people are reinventing now.
QR, NFC and the “UUID + URL” combination: it lacked global players, a partner network and simplicity.
A niche and academic life; the same ideas have been reinvented as DID, GS1/EPCIS and verifiable credentials.

A global resolver for physical objects: a ucode-like ID plus owner plus event history, resilient to a vendor disappearing. Needed by supply chains, repair, the secondary market and verifiable certificates — and still not built.

links.build: the fourth build decision: an identifier without a vendor

actions.t: Design an object resolver
actions.p: Design a resolver for physical objects: the ID format, the owner, the event history, and what happens when a vendor disappears. Compare with DID and GS1/EPCIS.

actions.t: Check ucode against sources
actions.p: Check the state of ucode/uID Center: alive or not, who uses it, what happened to T-Engine. Links to primary sources.

sources: Archive entry: ucode / Ubiquitous ID (verified by Archivessa)

iapx432.title: iAPX 432 — rights as architecture, not as discipline
iapx432.subtitle: 1981 — 1985 · Intel · a capability computer

fields.val: Intel's first 32-bit processor: a capability architecture with objects and descriptors, garbage collection and multitasking in hardware and microcode, a stack model with no visible registers; the primary OS and language were iMAX 432 and Ada.
A price and performance gap versus the 8086, no compilers, no backward compatibility; the capability mechanism came to be seen as “overhead”.
Dead, but the ideas were reborn: CHERI and ARM Morello, seL4, EROS/KeyKOS, WASI capabilities, Fuchsia.

Rights as transferable references instead of bearer tokens: an agent can call only what it was explicitly given and cannot “fetch” anything by name. A direct answer to the class of prompt-injection attacks and to an agent with full root access.

links.build: the fifth build decision: capability rights

other.agent-protocols/genmagic: Telescript also gave rights to an agent — at the language level

actions.t: Design a capability model for an agent
actions.p: Design a capability model for my agent: which references it receives, how it passes them on, how they are revoked, what happens under prompt injection. Compare with bearer tokens and ACLs.

actions.t: What is actually ready in CHERI/Morello
actions.p: Check the state of CHERI and ARM Morello: what is available to a developer today, which OSes support it, whether there is volume hardware. Primary sources with links.

transputer.title: Transputer — concurrency as physics
transputer.subtitle: 1983/1984 — 1990s · Inmos · CSP in silicon, Occam

fields.val: Inmos's British architecture (announced 1983, shipped 1984): a processor with four links and a hardware scheduler for CSP processes, the Occam language, TRAM modules. The flagship T9000 never shipped.
Concurrency as physics: processes and CSP channels in silicon, “a processor is a network node”, deterministic parallelism without an OS. Architecturally ahead of its time.
It demanded rewriting the world in Occam: no market, not enough money or marketing, T9000 was late and failed — cheap mass-market x86 won.
Dead, but CSP came back: Go, Erlang, Rust async. “A network of processors” is relevant again in chiplets and edge clusters.

Bring back the hardware honesty of CSP: guaranteed channel latency and a compiler that lays a program out across chiplets and nodes. Today this is assembled by hand through MPI and actors — and for multi-die and edge AI it is the key.

links.build: the sixth build decision: guaranteed channel latency
links.setun: both cards are about an architecture that outran the market

actions.t: Compare CSP channels with actors
actions.p: Compare CSP (Occam/Transputer, Go) with the actor model (Erlang/Akka): guarantees, latency, debugging, cost. What to take for multi-die and edge AI — with reasoning.

actions.t: Check the fate of the T9000
actions.p: Collect the facts on the Transputer and T9000 history: dates, reasons for failure, what became of Inmos. Links are mandatory.

setun.title: Setun — the ternary computer that came back in quantisation
setun.subtitle: 1958/1959 — 1965 · Moscow State University, Sobolev and Brusentsov · about 50 machines

fields.val: A computer on balanced ternary logic (Moscow State University; designed in 1958, produced 1959–1965 at the Kazan plant, about 50 machines; the successor was Setun-70).
Industrial inertia and politics: the binary direction had industry backing, the ternary line was left without production or development.
Ternary arithmetic is more economical than binary in representation density, rounds without accumulating error, and has a natural “−1 / 0 / +1” instead of two values.

Ternarity returned to ML in a different form: weights {−1, 0, +1} in 1.58-bit models are Setun in new clothing. Next: hardware for ternary and ternary-quantised inference, and ternary voting in consensus and recommendation systems.

links.transputer: both architectures lost the market but came back in another shape
links.build: the seventh build decision: a numeric representation for the task

actions.t: Check where ternary hardware stands
actions.p: Check what exists today for ternary and low-bit inference on hardware (1.58-bit models, research chips): facts and links, no forecasts.

actions.t: Compute the gain of ternary representation
actions.p: Compute in Python: how many weights fit into a memory budget with 16-bit versus ternary representation for a 1-billion-parameter model, and what the accumulation error is. Show the calculation.

msx.title: MSX — one specification, many manufacturers
msx.subtitle: 1983 — 1993 · ASCII + Microsoft · 14+ vendors

fields.val: A home-computer standard (ASCII + Microsoft, announced 27 June 1983): more than 14 manufacturers (Sony, Panasonic, Philips, Canon, Samsung and others), MSX BASIC/MSX-DOS, cartridges.
The first honest attempt at “one spec, many vendors”: a cartridge worked on any machine. Huge in Japan, Europe, Brazil and Korea — almost invisible in the US.
A late start and the wrong market; vendors did not want to lose differentiation; by the late 1980s it was displaced by PC clones and consoles. The last line was MSX turboR, 1993.
Dead outside the retro community.
The “common specification plus many manufacturers” model is exactly what edge modules and RISC-V devices need: backward compatibility as a product (a module that works everywhere).

links.pc98: the opposite strategy: a closed vertical
links.build: the eighth build decision: compatibility as a product

other.legacy-os/itron: the same “spec instead of product” model, and there it worked

actions.t: Compare MSX and RISC-V as models
actions.p: Compare the MSX model (one spec, many vendors) with the RISC-V ecosystem: what they share, why one died in 1993 while the other lives. Source links.

pc98.title: PC-98 — why a local standard always loses
pc98.subtitle: 1982 — 2003 · NEC · 18.3 million machines

fields.val: The NEC PC-9800: 18.3 million machines; x86-compatible but hardware-closed Japanese PCs with their own graphics for kanji, N88-BASIC and MS-DOS.
DOS/V (1990) let IBM clones draw Japanese text in software — and isolation turned into collapse: the market moved to the global standard. Production ended on 30 September 2003.
Dead; the platform is an object of collecting and emulation.
Separate localisation from the core: keyboard layouts, typography and legal formats as a plug-in layer; bus, APIs and data formats global. Protectionism at the format level always loses.

links.msx: successful compatibility against a closed vertical
links.troncode: the same dispute: local precision against a global standard
links.build: the ninth build decision: what to localise and what not

actions.t: Check my product for the PC-98 trap
actions.p: Check my product for the “PC-98 trap”: what in it is locally specific, what should be a plug-in, and what must be global. Give a list of decisions.

actions.t: Take apart the DOS/V story
actions.p: Establish from sources how DOS/V broke the PC-98 market: dates, technical details, NEC's reaction. Links are mandatory.

troncode.title: TRON Code — a character variant as a separate identifier
troncode.subtitle: 1980s — present · TRON · no Han unification

fields.val: TRON's own multi-byte encoding: every ideograph from every national set (JIS, GB 2312, Big5, KS X 1001) is encoded separately — without the Han unification adopted by Unicode.
Precise CJK typography: it is impossible to confuse a Japanese, Chinese and Korean form of a character; historical and archaic variants are separate characters rather than “the same symbol”.

To global Unicode and the economics of fonts: the TRON set required more than 200,000 code points, the fonts had restrictions on commercial use, and the encoding could not keep up with Unicode extensions.
A niche: fonts and data in the TRON ecosystem. Unicode solved part of the problem with variation selectors (IVS).

For legally significant texts and localisation, bring back “a variant as a separate identifier”: variant tags in the data plus provenance for the character's origin. In the ML age this is also correct CJK tokenisation without losing the glyph.

links.pc98: the same fork: local precision against a global format
links.build: the tenth build decision: a variant as data

other.legacy-os/tron: the encoding is part of the TRON project: the same argument about precision

actions.t: Check my CJK handling
actions.p: Check how my project handles CJK: where a character variant is lost, what to do about variation selectors, how to store the provenance of a glyph. Give concrete changes.

actions.t: Take apart Han unification
actions.p: Explain from sources what Han unification in Unicode is, what problems it creates for typography, and how IVS partly solves it. Links are mandatory.

news.title: NeWS — send a program, not a picture
news.subtitle: 1986 — 1993 · Sun · the window server as a PostScript interpreter

fields.val: Sun's window system (by James Gosling and David Rosenthal): the window server as a PostScript interpreter — the client sends a program, not pixels.
The display as a computer: an extensible server, server-side rendering, small channels; an ideal model for thin clients and remote interfaces.
X11 won on politics and price: X code was given away free, NeWS was licensed; OPEN LOOK lost to Motif and Sun dropped support.
Dead, but the techniques live on in shaders and GPU compute, in server-side rendering and in interface streaming.

Send a program, not a picture — an ideal model for remote and AI-generated interfaces: the server or agent ships a declarative description, the client only executes and collects input. Less traffic, more control.

links.weiser: both cards are about how an interface should behave in the background
links.build: the eleventh build decision: a declarative UI

actions.p: Design a protocol by which an agent delivers an interface declaratively (not pixels and not arbitrary HTML): what can be described, how the client executes it, where the security boundaries are.

actions.t: Take apart the NeWS story

weiser.title: Weiser — information without interruption
weiser.subtitle: 1991 — present · Xerox PARC · calm technology

fields.val: A Xerox PARC programme and the paper “The Computer for the 21st Century” (1991): tabs, pads and boards — computers the size of a sticky note, a sheet and a whiteboard; “the constant background of information requires no active attention, yet is ready for a glance”.
A rejection of the “personal computer” idea: technology should recede into the background and free attention. The most humane formulation of what we now call IoT.

Implemented partly and badly: connectivity exists, calm does not — attention became a commodity and ubicomp platforms degenerated into surveillance systems. This is the main critique of Weiser's legacy.

Information without interruption: ambient and glanceable surfaces (e-ink, panels, audio cues) plus the rule of when to stay silent. For agents this is a normative principle: an agent stays silent until the decision changes, instead of reporting every step.

links.news: the interface as background: two sides of one idea
links.build: the twelfth build decision: the rule of silence

actions.t: Write the rule of silence for an agent
actions.p: Write the normative rule of “when an agent stays silent”: which events do not warrant a notification, what counts as a change of decision, what a glanceable status looks like. Start from calm technology.

build.title: Build: a device and a protocol that survive
build.subtitle: the stack's practical output · 11 decisions from 11 cards

fields.lbl: An open licence and a low entry bar
fields.val: What survives is what can be repeated over a weekend: QR was opened — and it has lived for 30 years.
Payment and access are physical infrastructure: they work without a network, answer in a fixed time, and keep cryptography in the chip.
An object ID is separated from the carrier and the application; resolution is two-stage and data outlives the company.
Rights are transferable references, not strings and ACLs. An agent cannot “fetch” what it was not given.
Concurrency as a platform property, not a library: channels and a scheduler with predictable behaviour.

fields.lbl: A numeric representation for the task
fields.val: Ternarity and low-bit arithmetic are not exotica but a memory and energy budget; do the arithmetic before choosing hardware.
Compatibility as a product: the module works everywhere, the vendor adds only on top.

fields.lbl: Localisation as a plug-in, a global core
fields.val: Layouts and typography are a layer; data formats and APIs are global. Otherwise DOS/V comes for you.
A glyph, a form, a historical variant is a separate identifier with provenance, not “the same symbol”.
The agent ships a description (a program), the client executes it — less traffic and clear security boundaries.
An agent stays silent until the decision changes; attention is a scarce resource, not a delivery channel for statuses.
